topic: Production Python architecture: domain models, repositories, DI, packaging
why: An FDE writes code that the customer's own engineers will own six weeks after the engagement ends, so the real deliverable is not the feature but a codebase a stranger can extend in a day without calling you. The same service is deployed against different databases, secret stores and model providers per customer (Postgres here, Snowflake there; Anthropic direct here, Bedrock behind a gateway there), which is only cheap if persistence, config and LLM calls sit behind ports that the composition root wires up. Take-home graders at Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks read your module layout, your pyproject.toml and your tests before they run anything; a flat script with SQLAlchemy models as the domain model is the most common reason a strong candidate gets a 'no'.
prerequisites: Python 3.11+ fluency: type hints and generics, dataclasses, context managers, decorators, generators, `__eq__`/`__hash__` semantics, how `import` executes module code
SQL and Postgres basics (a table, a transaction, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) from 'AWS data: RDS Postgres, S3, ElastiCache, DynamoDB' (topic 14); the deep planner work in topic 29 is not required yet
pytest basics: writing a test file, fixtures, `-k`, `-x`, `--lf`; the property-testing and contract material in topic 35 builds on what you do here
Docker multi-stage images and non-root containers from 'Production images and supply chain' (topic 6), because the packaging subtopics end in a Dockerfile
Git branch hygiene from topic 4 so the restructure of the Kaupex Task Compiler lands as a reviewable series of small commits rather than one 3,000-line diff
Read access to the current Kaupex Task Compiler code and a written list of its three worst pain points (where a change today touches the most files)

subtopics.name: Layers and the dependency rule, enforced by the build
subtopics.learn: Draw the four layers you will use for every service: domain (pure Python, no I/O), service layer (use cases that orchestrate domain objects through ports), adapters (SQLAlchemy, HTTP clients, LLM SDKs, filesystem), entrypoints (FastAPI routes, Temporal activities, CLI). The rule is that imports only point inward: domain imports nothing from the other three, service imports domain and port interfaces only, adapters implement ports, entrypoints wire everything. Encode the rule as an import-linter contract in pyproject.toml (`[tool.importlinter]` with `root_package = "kaupex"` and a `type = "layers"` contract listing `kaupex.entrypoints`, `kaupex.adapters`, `kaupex.service_layer`, `kaupex.domain` top to bottom) and run `lint-imports` in CI so a `from sqlalchemy import ...` inside `domain/` fails the build instead of a code review.

resource.label: Import Linter documentation (layers and forbidden contracts)

subtopics.name: Entities and value objects with dataclasses
subtopics.learn: Model value objects as `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)` so equality is by value, instances are hashable and usable as dict keys and set members, and accidental mutation raises `FrozenInstanceError`. Model entities with identity: keep `eq=False` or override `__eq__` to compare on the id field and set `__hash__` accordingly, because the default dataclass `__eq__` on all fields makes two snapshots of the same task unequal. Use `field(default_factory=list)` for mutable defaults, `kw_only=True` to make constructors readable in the service layer, and `__post_init__` to assert invariants (a `TaskSpec` with an empty step list is never constructible). Know the cost model: `slots=True` cuts per-instance memory roughly in half and blocks `__dict__` monkeypatching in tests, which is what you want in the domain.

resource.label: Python docs - dataclasses

subtopics.name: Typed identifiers, domain exceptions and invariants
subtopics.learn: Give every identifier its own type with `typing.NewType("TaskId", str)` so mypy rejects passing a `TenantId` where a `TaskId` belongs; the cost is zero at runtime. Build one exception hierarchy rooted at `class KaupexError(Exception)` with `DomainError`, `NotFound`, `Conflict`, `InvalidTransition` subclasses, raise them from the domain with `raise ... from exc` to preserve the chain, and attach diagnostic context with `exc.add_note(...)` (3.11+) rather than string-formatting it into the message. The entrypoint layer is the only place that translates them to HTTP 404/409/422 or a Temporal non-retryable failure. Never `except Exception` in domain or service code; catching at the edge with the full chain intact is what makes the customer's stack traces readable.

resource.label: Python tutorial - user-defined exceptions and exception chaining

subtopics.name: Pydantic at the boundary, dataclasses in the core
subtopics.learn: Pydantic `BaseModel` belongs where untrusted or external-shaped data enters: request bodies, LLM structured outputs, config files, webhook payloads. Use `model_validate` for dicts, `model_validate_json` for raw bytes (faster, skips a Python dict), `model_dump(mode="json")` for serialisation, and `ConfigDict(extra="forbid", frozen=True)` so unknown fields from a customer integration fail loudly rather than silently. Write explicit `to_domain()` on the schema and `from_domain()` classmethods rather than passing pydantic models into the service layer: validation-on-construction on every internal object is a measurable CPU cost in a hot compile loop, and an API field rename should never force a domain change. Know `field_validator` vs `model_validator(mode="after")` for cross-field rules that are about shape (boundary) versus rules that are about business meaning (domain `__post_init__`).

resource.label: Pydantic docs - Models

subtopics.name: Ports as Protocols versus ABCs
subtopics.learn: Define ports (repository, unit of work, LLM client, clock) as `typing.Protocol` classes so adapters conform structurally without inheriting anything, which is what lets you wrap a customer's existing client class untouched. Understand how mypy checks conformance: it is verified at assignment sites, so put `_: TaskRepository = SqlAlchemyTaskRepository(session)` in a test module to get a compile-time conformance check for every adapter. Use `@runtime_checkable` only for `isinstance` at the composition root, and know it checks method names, not signatures. Reach for `abc.ABC` with `@abstractmethod` instead when the port carries shared behaviour (a `seen` set that collects events, a template method) or when you want instantiation of an incomplete adapter to fail at construction rather than at first call.

resource.label: mypy docs - Protocols and structural subtyping

subtopics.name: The Repository pattern and its fake
subtopics.learn: A repository exposes collection semantics (`add(task)`, `get(task_id)`, `list_for_tenant(tenant_id, limit, after)`) and hides the query language; the service layer never sees a `Session` or a `select()`. Write the in-memory `FakeTaskRepository` backed by a dict first and keep it in `tests/` or `kaupex/adapters/fakes.py`, because it is what lets 90 percent of your tests run without Postgres. Resist the drift into a generic `filter(**kwargs)` method that reintroduces query logic into callers; add named methods for real use cases and let read-heavy reporting bypass the repository entirely (the CQRS split is a later concern). Decide up front how the repository exposes locking (`get_for_update(task_id)` mapping to `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) and pagination (keyset by `(created_at, id)`, never `OFFSET`), because those are the two things customers ask for in week two.

resource.label: Architecture Patterns with Python - Chapter 2: Repository Pattern

subtopics.name: Persistence mapping: imperative mapping vs translator objects
subtopics.learn: Two viable ways to keep SQLAlchemy out of the domain. Imperative (classical) mapping with `registry.map_imperatively(Task, task_table)` attaches ORM instrumentation to your plain dataclass so the domain file has zero SQLAlchemy imports; the cost is that mapped attributes gain lazy-loading behaviour and `__eq__` on dataclasses interacts with the identity map. The alternative is declarative `TaskRow(Base)` models plus explicit `to_domain()`/`from_domain()` translators in the adapter, which is more code but has no magic and survives a customer's existing schema conventions. Either way learn the `Session` lifecycle: `sessionmaker(expire_on_commit=False)` so returned objects are usable after commit, the identity map (one Python object per primary key per session), and why a lazy-loaded relationship in a loop is an N+1 you fix with `selectinload` in the repository, not in the service.

resource.label: SQLAlchemy 2.0 ORM - Mapping styles (declarative and imperative)

subtopics.name: Unit of Work: one transaction per use case
subtopics.learn: The Unit of Work is a context manager that owns the session and exposes repositories: `with uow: uow.tasks.add(task); uow.commit()`. Implement `__enter__` to open a session from an injected `session_factory`, `__exit__` to `rollback()` unconditionally (a no-op after a successful commit, the safety net after an exception), and make `commit()` explicit so partial work is never persisted by accident. Build `FakeUnitOfWork` with a `committed` boolean so service-layer tests assert `assert uow.committed` instead of inspecting a database. Rule for FDE work: exactly one `with uow` per service function, never nested, and never held open across a network call to an LLM or the customer's API, because a 20-second model call inside an open transaction is how you create `idle in transaction` connection exhaustion in Postgres.

resource.label: Architecture Patterns with Python - Chapter 6: Unit of Work Pattern

subtopics.name: Service layer and the high-gear/low-gear testing decision
subtopics.learn: Service functions take primitives or DTOs plus a unit of work (`compile_task(task_id: str, uow: AbstractUnitOfWork, llm: LLMClient) -> CompileResult`), load aggregates through repositories, call domain methods, commit, and return plain data; they never contain `if` statements about business rules, only orchestration. Write the majority of tests against this layer with fakes: it is fast, it survives domain refactors, and it tests the same path every entrypoint will call. Keep a small number of domain unit tests for genuinely tricky rules and delete domain tests that merely duplicate a service test. Every new entrypoint (FastAPI route in topic 26, Temporal activity in topic 34, CLI here) becomes a ten-line adapter over the same service function, which is the property that makes 'add a batch mode' a one-day task for the customer's engineer.

resource.label: Architecture Patterns with Python - Chapter 4: Service Layer

subtopics.name: Aggregates, consistency boundaries and optimistic concurrency
subtopics.learn: An aggregate is the one object a use case loads, mutates and saves in a transaction; for the Task Compiler that is a `Task` with its steps, not each step individually. Choose the boundary by asking which invariants must be true at commit time (no two steps with the same ordinal, total steps under the plan limit); anything not in that set can be eventually consistent. Protect the aggregate with a `version_number` column: the repository's UPDATE includes `WHERE id = :id AND version_number = :expected` and raises `Conflict` when rowcount is 0, so two workers compiling the same task cannot silently produce a lost update. Know when to use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (short critical sections, high contention) instead, and write the test that spawns two threads against a real Postgres and asserts exactly one wins.

resource.label: Architecture Patterns with Python - Chapter 7: Aggregates and Consistency Boundaries

subtopics.name: Dependency injection with a composition root, no framework
subtopics.learn: All wiring lives in one `bootstrap.py`: it builds the session factory from settings, constructs adapters (`AnthropicLLMClient(api_key=settings.anthropic_key.get_secret_value())`, `SqlAlchemyUnitOfWork(session_factory)`), and returns a bus or a dict of service callables with dependencies bound via `functools.partial` or closures. Constructor injection everywhere: a service or adapter receives its collaborators as `__init__` arguments and never reaches for a module-level global or `os.environ`. Inject the things that make tests nondeterministic or slow: `clock: Callable[[], datetime]`, `id_factory: Callable[[], TaskId]`, the LLM client, the HTTP session. Understand why module-level singletons (`client = anthropic.Anthropic()` at import) are a production bug and not just a test smell: they read secrets at import time, cannot be per-tenant, and are shared across forked workers. FastAPI's `Depends` (topic 26) is a thin wrapper over exactly this composition root.

resource.label: Architecture Patterns with Python - Chapter 13: Dependency Injection and Bootstrapping

subtopics.name: Settings: typed, validated once, secrets never in logs
subtopics.learn: One `Settings(BaseSettings)` class with `model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix="KAUPEX_", env_file=".env", env_nested_delimiter="__", extra="forbid")`, typed fields (`database_url: PostgresDsn`, `anthropic_api_key: SecretStr`, `llm_timeout_s: float = 30`), constructed exactly once in the composition root and passed down. Validation at startup means a missing or malformed variable fails the process in the first second with a field name in the error, instead of failing the first customer request at 3 a.m. `SecretStr` prints as `**********` in `repr` and logs, so an accidental `logger.info(settings)` does not leak a key. Never read `os.environ` below the composition root; a grep for `os.environ` and `os.getenv` outside `config.py` and `bootstrap.py` should return nothing, and that grep belongs in CI.

resource.label: Pydantic docs - Settings management (pydantic-settings)

subtopics.name: Package layout, imports and the circular-import trap
subtopics.learn: Use the src layout (`src/kaupex/...`) so tests import the installed package, not the working directory, which catches missing files in the wheel and stray relative imports. Absolute imports only; a `TYPE_CHECKING` guard for imports used purely in annotations; and if two modules genuinely need each other you have a layering error, not an import problem. Keep `__init__.py` files nearly empty (re-exports with `__all__` at most) because heavy `__init__` work runs on every import including `mypy` and test collection. Add `src/kaupex/__main__.py` so `python -m kaupex` works even without the console script installed, and measure import cost with `python -X importtime -c 'import kaupex' 2>&1 | sort -t'|' -k2 -n | tail` when a Lambda or CLI cold start gets slow.

resource.label: Python Packaging User Guide - src layout vs flat layout

subtopics.name: pyproject.toml, uv and a reproducible environment
subtopics.learn: One `pyproject.toml` with a PEP 621 `[project]` table (`name`, `version`, `requires-python = ">=3.11"`, `dependencies` with lower bounds only), `[dependency-groups]` (PEP 735) for `dev` and `test` extras, `[build-system]` with `hatchling` or `setuptools`, and `[tool.*]` tables for ruff, mypy and pytest so there is exactly one config file to hand a customer. Use uv for the workflow: `uv lock` produces a cross-platform `uv.lock` that you commit, `uv sync --frozen` fails rather than silently re-resolving when the lock is stale, `uv run pytest` runs inside the project environment, `uv add --group dev ruff` edits pyproject and lock together, and `uv build` produces the wheel. Know the difference between a library (loose pins, no lockfile shipped) and an application (lockfile is the contract), and that the Kaupex Task Compiler is an application.

resource.label: uv docs - Working on projects

subtopics.name: Console scripts and entry-point plugins
subtopics.learn: Declare the CLI in `[project.scripts]` as `kaupex = "kaupex.entrypoints.cli:main"` so installing the wheel puts a `kaupex` executable on PATH with no shell wrapper. Expose extension points the customer can fill without forking you: `[project.entry-points."kaupex.compilers"]` in your pyproject, and in your customer's separate package a `my_compiler = "acme_kaupex.steps:AcmeStep"` line; discover them at bootstrap with `importlib.metadata.entry_points(group="kaupex.compilers")` and load with `.load()`. Read your own version at runtime with `importlib.metadata.version("kaupex")` and put it in the `/health` payload and every log line so a customer bug report tells you which build they run. Understand that entry points are resolved from installed distribution metadata, so a plugin that is on `sys.path` but not installed is invisible.

resource.label: Python Packaging User Guide - Entry points specification

subtopics.name: Static gates: mypy strict where it pays, ruff everywhere
subtopics.learn: Configure mypy in pyproject with `strict = true` for `kaupex.domain` and `kaupex.service_layer` via `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]` `module = ["kaupex.domain.*", "kaupex.service_layer.*"]`, and relax to `disallow_untyped_defs = false` plus `ignore_missing_imports` for adapters wrapping untyped vendor SDKs; a blanket strict setting on day one produces 400 errors and gets disabled by the next engineer. Use `warn_unused_ignores` so stale `# type: ignore` comments are removed, and `plugins = ["pydantic.mypy"]` for correct model inference. Ruff replaces flake8, isort and black: `[tool.ruff.lint] select = ["E", "F", "I", "B", "UP", "N", "SIM"]`, `ruff check --fix` and `ruff format` in pre-commit, and `ruff check --output-format=github` in CI so violations annotate the PR. The whole gate must run in under a minute or engineers bypass it.

resource.label: mypy docs - The mypy configuration file (per-module overrides)

subtopics.name: Test architecture: unit, integration and end-to-end tiers
subtopics.learn: Three tiers with distinct speed budgets: `tests/unit/` uses fakes and finishes in under two seconds for the whole Task Compiler; `tests/integration/` hits a real Postgres (a `postgres_session` fixture with `scope="session"` that creates the schema once and wraps each test in a rolled-back transaction) and is marked `@pytest.mark.integration`; `tests/e2e/` drives the CLI or HTTP entrypoint. Layer fixtures in `conftest.py`: `settings` builds a test `Settings`, `session_factory` depends on it, `uow` depends on that, and a `bootstrap` fixture returns the fully wired service with a `FakeLLMClient` that replays recorded responses. Register markers in `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` with `markers = ["integration: needs postgres"]` and `addopts = "--strict-markers -m 'not integration'"` so the default run is fast and CI adds `-m integration` in a job that has the database. Mock only at the boundary you do not own; if you find yourself patching your own service functions, the dependency should have been injected.

resource.label: pytest docs - How to use fixtures (scopes, conftest, dependency chains)

subtopics.name: Logging as a cross-cutting concern with the right seams
subtopics.learn: Every module gets `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` and nothing else; configuration happens once in the entrypoint via `logging.config.dictConfig` with a JSON formatter in production and a human one locally. Correlation and tenant ids enter at the entrypoint (HTTP header, Temporal workflow id, CLI flag), are stored in a `contextvars.ContextVar`, and a `logging.Filter` copies them onto every `LogRecord`, so the domain and service layers never take a `request_id` parameter just to log it. Log domain events at INFO with structured fields (`extra={"task_id": ..., "step": ...}`) not f-strings, so the customer's log pipeline can index them; log at the adapter boundary for every external call with duration and outcome. Never log a full LLM prompt or response at INFO by default; put it behind a `KAUPEX_LOG_PROMPTS` setting that defaults to false because customer PII will be in there.

resource.label: Python Logging HOWTO (basic and advanced tutorial, filters, contextual information)

subtopics.name: Shipping the package as a container with uv
subtopics.learn: Multi-stage Dockerfile: a builder stage from `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv` copies `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` first and runs `uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-install-project` so the dependency layer caches independently of your source, then copies `src/` and runs `uv sync --frozen --no-dev` to install the project itself. Set `UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1` and `UV_LINK_MODE=copy` in the builder, copy only `/app/.venv` into a slim `python:3.12-slim` runtime stage, run as a non-root user, and start with `ENTRYPOINT ["/app/.venv/bin/kaupex"]` or `python -m kaupex` so signals reach PID 1. Verify the result: `docker run --rm image kaupex --version` prints the same version as `importlib.metadata`, and `uv pip list` inside the container matches `uv.lock` exactly. This is the artifact the customer's platform team will deploy on the EKS cluster from topic 16.

resource.label: uv docs - Using uv in Docker

subtopics.name: The second-engineer test: ADRs, CONTRIBUTING and the extension recipe
subtopics.learn: Write one Architecture Decision Record per structural choice you made this week (why dataclasses not pydantic in the domain, why imperative mapping or why translators, why uv, why optimistic locking) in `docs/adr/NNNN-title.md` with Context, Decision, Consequences; five short ADRs beat one design doc because the customer's engineer reads the one that answers their question. Write a `CONTRIBUTING.md` whose centrepiece is a numbered recipe, 'How to add a new compiler step', naming the exact files to touch in order (domain rule, service function, port change if any, adapter, fake, unit test, integration test, ADR if it changes a decision) with a real example diff linked. Then run the test: hand the repo to someone who has never seen it (or to yourself after a week away, using only the docs) and time how long it takes to add a trivial step with passing tests. Under a day is the target from the plan; under two hours means the architecture is doing its job.

resource.label: Architectural Decision Records (adr.github.io) - templates and guidance

outcomes: You can draw the four layers of the restructured Kaupex Task Compiler from memory, and `lint-imports` in CI fails the build when you deliberately add `from sqlalchemy import select` to a file under `kaupex/domain/`.

You can run the full service-layer test suite for the Task Compiler in under two seconds with no database and no network, using `FakeTaskRepository`, `FakeUnitOfWork` and a `FakeLLMClient`, and you can show `pytest -m integration` running the same use cases against a real Postgres.

You can swap the LLM adapter (Anthropic direct to LiteLLM or Bedrock) or the persistence adapter (Postgres to SQLite for a demo) with a diff that touches only `bootstrap.py` and one new adapter module, and the unchanged test suite proves the domain and service layers did not move.

You can clone the repo on a clean machine, run `uv sync --frozen && uv run kaupex --help`, and get a working CLI in under a minute; `uv lock --check` passes and `docker build` produces an image whose `kaupex --version` matches `importlib.metadata.version`.

You can explain for each of dataclass, pydantic model and SQLAlchemy model which layer it lives in, what specific thing breaks if you move it (validation cost, ORM coupling, schema-change blast radius), and defend that in a design review without appealing to 'best practice'.

You can demonstrate the optimistic-concurrency test: two threads compile the same task against Postgres, exactly one commits, the other raises `Conflict`, and you can point to the `WHERE version_number = :expected` clause that made it so.

`mypy` passes with `strict = true` on `kaupex.domain` and `kaupex.service_layer`, `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are clean, and the whole static gate runs in under a minute in pre-commit and CI.
A peer who has never seen the repo can follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` to add a new compiler step with unit and integration tests, and you have a timed record of them doing it in under a day.
failureModes: Pydantic models are used as the domain model and the ORM model at once: an API field rename for one customer forces a migration and a domain change, `extra="forbid"` starts rejecting rows with legacy columns, and profiling shows a third of compile-loop CPU in validators that re-check data already validated at the boundary.

A SQLAlchemy session is opened at module import or held open across a 20-second LLM call: Postgres fills with `idle in transaction` connections, `pg_stat_activity` shows the pool exhausted, autovacuum cannot clean the tables those transactions pin, and the first symptom the customer sees is `DetachedInstanceError` and timeouts three days later.

`client = anthropic.Anthropic()` at module scope reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` at import time: tests cannot inject a fake, the second tenant onboarded reuses the first tenant's key, and when gunicorn preloads the app the forked workers share one HTTP connection pool and start failing with SSL errors under load.

A circular import that only manifests through the CLI entrypoint's import order ships to production because the test suite imported modules in a different order; the container crash-loops with `ImportError: cannot import name ... (most likely due to a circular import)` and nobody can reproduce it locally until they run `python -m kaupex`.

No lockfile is committed and the Dockerfile runs `pip install -r requirements.txt` with lower bounds only: the customer rebuilds the image six weeks later, pulls a new pydantic or SQLAlchemy minor, and the service fails at startup with changed validation semantics while the FDE who wrote it is on another engagement.

The repository accumulates forty ad hoc query methods, then a developer bypasses it with a raw `session.execute(select(...))` in the service layer 'just this once'; within a quarter every service test needs Postgres, the suite takes fifteen minutes, engineers stop running it locally, and regressions reach the customer.

Business rules live in the FastAPI route handler and are duplicated into a Temporal activity when the customer asks for batch mode; the two copies drift, the batch path skips a validation the API enforces, and a month of compiled tasks has to be re-run after the customer's audit finds the inconsistency.
interviewQuestions: You inherit a 4,000-line Python service where the SQLAlchemy models are the domain model and business rules live in the route handlers; the customer needs a batch CLI over the same logic next sprint and will not accept a feature freeze. Walk me through the restructure in the order you would actually commit it, how you keep every commit shippable, and what evidence you show the customer that nothing regressed.

Explain Repository and Unit of Work as you would implement them in Python, then tell me when they are overkill. Where do you draw the line differently for a two-week FDE pilot versus a system you are handing to the customer's platform team, and what is the cheapest version that still lets you swap the database?

Pick Protocol or ABC for the port to an LLM provider that a customer might implement themselves, and defend it. How does mypy verify that their adapter conforms, where exactly does that check happen, and what happens at runtime if their class is missing a method?

Debug this: after your deploy, workers intermittently raise `DetachedInstanceError`, and the customer's DBA shows you 200 Postgres connections in `idle in transaction`. Which layer is the bug most likely in, what is your hypothesis about the code shape that causes it, and what change fixes it structurally rather than by raising `max_connections`?

Two Temporal workers can compile the same task concurrently. Design the persistence so that a lost update is impossible: optimistic versus pessimistic locking, where the version check lives in the layered architecture, how the conflict surfaces to the caller, and the exact test you would write to prove it.

A customer runs the same service in two environments with different secret stores (AWS Secrets Manager in one, HashiCorp Vault in the other) and different model providers. Show me how settings and the composition root make that a one-file change per environment, what you validate at process start, and what you deliberately defer to first use.

Walk me through how you package a Python service so a customer engineer can install, run and extend it without you: what is in pyproject.toml, what the lockfile is a contract for, how a console script and an entry-point plugin work, and how the Dockerfile is structured so a dependency change does not rebuild the source layer.
proofOfWork: A recorded 'second-engineer drill' on the restructured Kaupex Task Compiler. Before recording, tag the repo and check in a CI pipeline that runs `lint-imports`, `mypy`, `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `uv lock --check`, the unit tier with a two-second wall-clock budget asserted via `--durations=0` in the log, and the integration tier against a Postgres service container. Then hand the repo to a peer who has never seen it (or, failing that, to yourself after a week away with the diff hidden) and record them adding a new compiler step, for example 'reject any step whose prompt exceeds the tenant's token budget', using only `CONTRIBUTING.md`: they must touch the domain rule, a service function, the fake, a unit test and an integration test, and CI must go green. Alongside the recording, publish the diffstat of a second PR that swaps the LLM adapter from Anthropic direct to LiteLLM, showing that only `bootstrap.py`, `config.py` and one new file under `adapters/` changed and that the test suite ran unchanged, plus the five ADRs that explain why the architecture is shaped the way it is. The timing of the drill, the diffstat and the ADRs together are the evidence that a stranger can extend the service in a day and that you can say why.
